package_info.package_versions: Custom malicious images based on TP-Link WR940N v6 (and possibly others)
package_info.why_malicious: The firmware contains a persistent backdoor (Horse Shell) that grants attackers remote shell access, file transfer, and tunneling capabilities, while disabling legitimate firmware upgrades to maintain persistence. It is designed for covert control and proxying, not for any legitimate router function.

execution_context.file_location: Custom binary in SquashFS filesystem (Horse Shell implant)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Upon initialization, the Horse Shell backdoor implant directs the operating system to run as a daemon in the background and ignore termination commands such as SIGPIPE, SIGINT, SIGABRT.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At boot-time, the code launches a persistent daemon process that ignores termination signals, ensuring the backdoor remains running and cannot be easily killed.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Legitimate router processes do not typically run hidden daemons that ignore all termination signals.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal router firmware does not spawn persistent, unkillable background processes unrelated to routing functions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some critical system daemons may ignore certain signals for stability, but not in this covert manner.
key_indicators: Daemon process not present in official firmware
Runs in background without user visibility

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Upon connecting to the C2 server, the backdoor sends the victim’s machine profile: user name, OS version, time, device information, IP address, MAC address, supported implant features.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after establishing a C2 connection, the code collects system and network information and exfiltrates it to the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unsolicited exfiltration of device and user information to an external server is a hallmark of backdoor malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate firmware does not send detailed device profiles to unknown external servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some telemetry or support features may send limited data to vendor servers, but not to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
key_indicators: Exfiltration of sensitive device and user data

execution_context.file_location: Horse Shell binary (remote shell module, using Telnet library)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The malware grants threat actors complete device control, enabling them to execute commands, transfer files, and utilize it as a SOCKS proxy for communication relay.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C (embedded Linux binary, leveraging Telnet and SOCKS libraries)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving C2 instructions, the code spawns a remote shell, allows file transfer, and sets up a SOCKS proxy, enabling full remote control and use of the device as a relay node.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote shell, file transfer, and proxying are not legitimate features for consumer router firmware and enable covert attacker operations.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Routers should not provide arbitrary shell access or proxying to external parties.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote support features may allow limited access, but not full shell or proxying for arbitrary external use.
key_indicators: SOCKS proxy setup for traffic relay
File transfer functionality outside of firmware updates

execution_context.file_location: Modified web interface code in firmware

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The modified firmware restricts the device owner from updating the router’s firmware through the management web panel, thereby ensuring the infection remains persistent.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user attempts to access the firmware upgrade feature, the code disables or removes the upgrade option, preventing legitimate firmware restoration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Blocking firmware upgrades is a classic persistence technique for malware implants.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate firmware always allows the owner to upgrade or restore the device.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some ISPs may lock firmware for support reasons, but not in consumer devices without notice.
key_indicators: Firmware upgrade option missing or disabled
No legitimate way to restore original firmware via web panel

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains admin access to router (via exploit or weak credentials) and uploads malicious firmware.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious firmware is installed and device is rebooted.

attack_chain.action: Horse Shell implant initializes at boot, running as a persistent daemon and ignoring termination signals.
attack_chain.leads_to: Backdoor remains active and hidden on the device.

attack_chain.action: Backdoor establishes connection to C2 server and exfiltrates device profile information.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives device details and confirms successful infection.

attack_chain.action: On C2 command, Horse Shell provides remote shell, file transfer, and proxying capabilities.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can use device for lateral movement, data exfiltration, or as a relay node.

attack_chain.action: Firmware disables legitimate upgrade options to maintain persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Device owner cannot easily remove the implant.

behavioral_signatures: Persistent daemon process not present in official firmware
Unsolicited outbound connections to non-TP-Link servers
Remote shell or proxy services running on router
Web interface missing or disabling firmware upgrade options
file_indicators: Custom binaries in SquashFS filesystem not present in official images
Presence of open-source libraries (Telnet, libev, TOR smart list) in firmware
network_indicators: Outbound connections to attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure
SOCKS proxy traffic relayed through router
Unusual HTTP headers or traffic patterns matching open-source code
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor router firmware integrity and compare filesystem contents to official images. Look for persistent unknown processes, especially those ignoring termination signals. Detect outbound connections to suspicious C2 servers and the presence of remote shell or proxy services. Check if the firmware upgrade option is missing or disabled in the web interface. Use network monitoring to identify unexpected proxy or shell traffic.
